The repositioning of the United Nations Development System was not intended as an institutional exercise for its own sake. Its purpose was to enable the United Nations to deliver more effectively, more coherently, with greater accountability in support of the member states, the achievement of gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls in the broader Sustainable Development Goals. For UN Women, one of the greatest measures of whether this reform is succeeding is whether gender equality and women's empowerment is increasingly reflected in how the United Nations system plans its work, finances, and delivers collectively. This is particularly important given the UN General Assembly Resolution 64/289 that established UN Women, in which coordination is a core pillar of UN Women's triple mandate and recognized the importance of delivery at the global level at the regional level and at the country level. As UN Women, we continue to reposition ourselves within the broader development system, remaining focused on ensuring that gender equality is central to the collective United Nations action at all levels of the system. This matters because gender equality and women's rights and empowerment cannot be advanced by one entity alone. It requires coordinated policy support, coordinated joint action, integrated financing, stronger data and evidence, collective accountability for results. In many ways, it depends precisely on the capabilities of the member states to strengthen through development system reform and support. The Executive Director's report on the first day of this board highlighted important progress across several dimensions of the reform agenda. At the country level, the engagement with the UNCTSWAP has more than doubled, increasing by 105% from 61 countries to 125 countries in 2025. This reflects growing ownership of gender equality commitments across the resident coordinators in the United Nations country teams. Today, more than 100 gender theme groups across 136 United Nations country teams are helping translate global and interagency commitments into country-level programs aligned with national priorities under the leadership of the resident coordinators with support of UN Women. These mechanisms remain particularly important in context where UN Women operates through multi-country offices or where UN system presence and capabilities vary, helping extend accountability and coordination beyond UN Women's physical footprint. The reports also points to improvement in accountability for gender equality across 75 United Nations entities, contributing to a stronger uptake of norms, standards, and consistent integration of gender equality across development, humanitarian and peacebuilding efforts. This is particularly important given the increasing interconnected nature of development, humanitarian and peace contexts, including fragile settings in small island developing states facing structural vulnerabilities. The report further highlights progress through the Secretary-General's Gender Equality Acceleration Plan. The Gender Equality Acceleration Plan is helping sharpen leadership, accountability, and financing across the system whilst accelerating implementation to commitments already made. At country level, it also supports UN Women's dual role of influencing cooperation frameworks and system-wide priorities while UN Women delivers on its own programs through the strategy notes aligned with national development objectives. At the same time, the reports remind us that progress cannot be taken for granted amid persistent regressions, stagnations, and pushback on gender equality. The share of United Nations Development Cooperation Frameworks integrating gender equality declined from 66% in 2022 to 61% in 2025. This only reinforces the importance of a strong and well-functioning gender equality architecture across the United Nations system. At a time when progress is uneven and resources are constrained, mechanisms of coordination, accountability, and collective action become even much more important. The collective challenge to us is to ensure that these mechanisms continue to drive implementation at country level, and therefore our strong commitment that cooperation framework should have a gender outcome in addition to mainstreaming UN Women. This is where UN Women's precise coordination mandate adds value and builds on the commitments that you member states already made through the UNCTSWAP and the UN SWAP and the Gender Equality Marker and other tools. The report highlights how UN Women's coordination mandate contributes to the broader architecture and the interagency Network on Gender Equality that is established by ECOSOC. We are pleased to share with you that we continue to strengthen this ECOSOC-mandated structure which supports development cooperation, and we will have an assistant level interagency network so that we are able to build into recommendations into the High Level Committee on Programme. Excellencies, building on these efforts, UN Women is clear that pooled funds of the United Nations, like the Peace Building Fund, the SDG Fund, are critical mechanisms that must continue to incorporate gender equality. UN Women is also drawing on the findings of the Rapid Synthesis Evaluation on coordination, and yesterday you spent time discussing evaluations, and I'm pleased to inform that for us this is very important, and in this regard, we really appreciate the Executive Director's decision to establish coordination specialists at the regional level in all our regional offices that have really seen us strengthen our work. As you advised in the last two days, and as we continue on the discussions on UNAT, UN Women remains very strongly involved in the country configuration and regional reset discussions, and we remain helping shape a more coherent, effective, and context-specific response that centers gender equality and coordination within that effort, maximizing on the lessons learned and scaling up on opportunities. I would like, with this introduction, to invite, to welcome through you, Mr. President, Alice Shekhofid, the Director of the Coordination Division, acting and interim, to provide a detailed update and again to extend our appreciation for the support that the Board continues to provide and the guidance on this critical aspect of our triple mandate coordination. Your Excellency, distinguished delegates and colleagues, it is an honor to share from our global office in Nairobi the highlights of our contribution to the repositioned United Nations Development System for our unique triple mandate. Three things I will share with you today. First, we must recognize that UN Women as a unique dual role as an active member of the UN development system and as a lead entity on gender equality, leveraging the entire UN system. UN Women brings the gender equality expertise, normative grounding, and coordination function that enable large programs led by different agencies of the UN system to deliver more coherently for women and girls. There is a clear multiplier effect of UN Women's coordination mandate, and through our strong engagement with resident coordinators, UN country teams, agency funds and programs, as well as regional collaborative platform, we serve as a knowledge hub on gender equality, providing leadership standards, technical expertise at global, regional, and country level. In 2025, the UN achieved gender parity in international professional and higher categories for the first time. 27 out of 38 UN entities now reaching parity, up from 5 in 2017. UN Women led this process by supporting the system-wide strategy on gender parity. Second, our contribution extends well beyond, beyond our programs and strengthens the entire UN system. Therefore, when you Member States invest in UN Women, you are not only investing in one entity's program, you are investing in the connective tissue that enables the broader UN system to deliver more coherently on gender equality and women's rights through the UN system gender equality architecture. We are currently guiding and supporting 75 UN entities and 126 UNCTs through the implementation of system-wide action plans on gender, including gender parity standards and gender markers, as mentioned by our Deputy Executive Director. UN Women's coordination mandate has been further reinforced by the 2024 Secretary General's System-Wide Gender Equality Acceleration Plan, which was launched to accelerate progress on gender equality and empowerment of women. Our strategic planning documents are 100% aligned to cooperation frameworks, and our representatives at country level regularly report to resident coordinators in line with the management accountability framework. The course I Know Gender has strengthened the knowledge of more than 45,000 UN personnel worldwide, and our leading role in UN country teams to advance on the implementation of the, of the, of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women has translated in 99% of the UN country team submitting ports since 2022. Now we know very well the resident coordinator leadership is critical to advance gender equality, and that's why we work very closely with the Development Cooperation— Coordination Office at the global and regional level, and we have met our funding obligations of $2.7 million in 2025. At the same time, UN Women country offices participate in 80% of active business operation strategy management, and 76% of our offices are co-located in UN common premises. The increased use of common services and common back office solutions has generated efficiency gains and cost savings of $15.2 million. This is 3.8 times higher of what we reported last year. Third point, and last, While progress is evident, it is not guaranteed. Efforts remain uneven and in some cases are at risk of regression. Sustained leadership, adequate resourcing, and stronger collaboration, particularly at country level with resident coordinators, are essential to maintain momentum, prevent duplication, and ensure that gender equality remains a system-wide priority in cooperation frameworks and in other plans like humanitarian response plans. And in the case of cooperation frameworks, as mentioned by Dede, only 71% mainstream gender in 2025. And together with that challenge, we must ensure with your leadership adequate and predictable financing for gender equality commitments under the Funding Compact. As UN Women, we are committed to achieving gender equality, and under your leadership and in partnership with civil society and partners, We are committed to advance the 2030 Agenda, respond to humanitarian crisis, and ensure peace and security. Thank you for your continued partnership and support. Over to you, Mr. President.

Thank you, Mr. President, Excellencies. I deliver this statement on behalf of the following Member States: Albania, Australia, Belgium, Canada, Czech Republic, Denmark, Germany, Iceland, Ireland, Japan, Luxembourg, Republic of Moldova, Montenegro, the Kingdom of Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, United Kingdom, the EU as a donor, and my own country, Finland. We share the ambition to make the UN Development System more coherent, effective, efficient, and impactful at country level. UN Women is central to that ambition. Since the adoption of General Assembly Resolution 72/279, progress has been made and UN Women has played a constructive role. Yet the system is still not delivering on its full potential. Fragmentation, competition for funding, and weak incentives for collaboration continue to undermine collective impact. In a context of lagging SDG progress, growing humanitarian needs, and constrained ODA, This is not sustainable. We need a UN that acts as one UN in country, under the leadership of empowered resident coordinators, with UN Women as fully engaged and supportive partner. The UN80 initiative offers a unique opportunity to accelerate and strengthen the implementation of the repositioning of the UNDS launched in 2017. We ask all UN entities, including UN Women, to actively engage and show ownership of efforts under UN80 Workstream 3, through concrete steps. First, ensure UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks are the real drivers of UN Women's country work. The cooperation framework should be the single costed system-wide strategy at country level, in line with national priorities. Entity-specific country programme instruments must be genuinely derived from, and not loosely aligned with, cooperation frameworks. Sequencing the finalisation of entity country programme instruments after finalisation of the cooperation frameworks should be the standard. As Executive Board, we can work with entities to help with sequencing while protecting programme delivery. We encourage UN Women to ensure its country-level reporting clearly captures its contribution to cooperation framework results and joint UN outcomes, not only agency-specific outputs. It is also key that UN Women ensures live work plans and resource pipelines are visible to the RC throughout implementation.. And our question here would be, what more could UN Women do at global, regional, and country level to further elevate the cooperation frameworks as central strategic frameworks? Then second, consistently and fully support Resident Coordinator and Humanitarian Coordinator leadership. This includes recognizing the RCHC as the default strategic interlocutor for high-level engagement with government and donors, systematically involving the RC in major strategic decisions and ensuring that project proposals agreed directly with donors are fully in line to the cooperation framework and are shared with the RC HC in advance. The question here would be whether you could share which challenges UN Women faces that limit your ability to do so. We also support a stronger role for RCs in the selection and performance assessments of country representatives. Country representatives should be assessed based on their contribution to collective results, and the delivery of the cooperation framework. We call on UN Women to more systematically request and integrate RC feedback into the performance assessments of country representatives. Third, tailor agency in-country presence to national contexts, comparative advantage, and the needs identified in the cooperation framework in consultation with RCs and host governments. This remains a key unfinished element of UNDS reform. We encourage UN Women to draw the system-wide evaluation on progress towards a new generation on UNCTs and meaningfully contribute to the UN Country Team reconfiguration. Fourth, advance shared services. We are encouraged by the system-wide efficiency gains of over $980 million USD in 2025 and count on UN Women to build on this progress to make shared services, common back offices, and co-location the norm. The number of common back offices at country level remains limited, and question here would be What, in your view, are the main obstacles to establishing common back offices, and do you have suggestions as how these obstacles could be overcome? Finally, we acknowledge that as member states we also have an important role. Funding practices must incentivize collaboration rather than fragmentation. The current imbalance between core and earmarked resources and the proliferation of short-term project-based funding undermines strategic planning and joint work. Beyond— and here comes a question— beyond funding, what is the one key change Member States can enact that would enable you to reduce competition and better align with cooperation frameworks? Mr. President, by fully embracing system-wide reforms, UN Women can enhance its impact and help the UN deliver as one where it matters most, most at country level. Thank you.

UN Women recognizes that effective safeguarding depends on meaningful engagement with and accountability to the communities we serve. Accordingly, we work closely with women-led and civil society organizations to ensure that safeguarding measures are informed by community voices and are responsive to local realities. At the core of our action is victim-survivor-centered approach, which respects the rights, wishes, needs, and dignity of victims and survivors, seeking to protect them from retaliation and re-traumatization and ensures provision of timely assistance and support. To operationalize these efforts at the regional and country level, we have established a strong network of 127 PSEH focal points across our global presence. Our approach is complemented by a strong focus on prevention and response, including awareness-raising, tracing, risk mitigation, including with implementing partners, and robust vetting and accountability measures. In 2025, we continue to expand entity-level outreach on SCA and SH.
